Package org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter

Class LoopbackBoundary

java.lang.Object
org.apache.juneau.rest.server.filter.LoopbackBoundary
All Implemented Interfaces:
RequestBoundary
public class LoopbackBoundary extends Object implements RequestBoundary
The request-authenticity half of a loopback application's write protection: decides whether a request came from the page this process served, and refuses it when it did not.
What this answers, and what it does not

An application bound to 127.0.0.1 is reachable only from this host, but "reachable only from this host" is not an authorization boundary — every browser the user has open is on this host, and any page in any of them can attempt a request to the port. This class answers exactly one question:

Did this request come from the page this process served?

It does not answer did the user mean it. A user who has the application's own page open, and who is induced to click something on it, produces a request that passes every check here. That is a question of intent, and it needs a separate, independent mechanism — a typed confirmation, an arming gate, a per-action phrase naming the specific target. The two gates are deliberately not combined, in this class or in its naming. Treating an intent gate as though it authenticated the request, or this boundary as though it established intent, is the specific confusion this separation exists to prevent: an application with only an arming gate is forgeable by any page in the browser, and an application with only this boundary will faithfully execute whatever its own page was tricked into asking for.

The checks
CheckApplies toRuleRejection
Hostevery request equals the configured authority exactly (over HTTP/2, the :authority; see below) 421 Misdirected Request
Originstate-changing requests present, and exactly http://<authority> 403 Forbidden
Sec-Fetch-Sitestate-changing requests absent, or exactly same-origin 403 Forbidden
Content-Typestate-changing requests base type is exactly application/json 415 Unsupported Media Type
CSRF tokenstate-changing requests the configured header equals the process's SynchronizerToken 403 Forbidden

A request is state-changing when its effective method is not safe (MethodSafety.effectiveMethod(String, String, java.util.function.UnaryOperator)): a GET carrying ?method=DELETE or an X-HTTP-Method-Override: PUT header takes the write checks, whether or not the resource it reaches would honour the override.

HTTP/2

An HTTP/2 request has no Host header; the container surfaces its :authority only as ServletRequest.getServerName() and ServletRequest.getServerPort(). A request with no Host whose ServletRequest.getProtocol() is exactly HTTP/2.0 is therefore judged on that server name and port, compared as a parsed host and port (an absent port is 80) rather than as text. A request that carries a Host header is compared as written, as always. A WebSocket handshake carried over HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) is judged the same way, on the authority of its request URI, through acceptsHandshakeHost(HandshakeHosts, String).

Residual risk. When an HTTP/2 request names no :authority at all, containers fill the server name with their own bound address, which is this boundary's authority when it is bound to loopback. A browser always sends :authority, so only a non-browser client can provoke this, and such a client must still present the Origin and token.

Why each check is present

Host on every request, not only writes. This is the check that defeats DNS rebinding, and it is the reason the boundary cannot be scoped to the write path. An attacker serves a page from http://evil.example with a very short DNS TTL, then re-resolves that name to 127.0.0.1. Requests the page then makes to http://evil.example/... are same-origin from the browser's point of view: no CORS, no preflight, Origin is the page's own origin and therefore consistent, and the response body is readable. Neither origin checking nor a CSRF token stops this — the page can simply fetch this application's own HTML and scrape the token out of it. What the attacker cannot change is the Host header, which after rebinding still carries evil.example.

Restricting that check to writes would leave every read surface open to the one attack it exists to stop, and a rebound page that can read the application's data tables is already an exfiltration problem whether or not it can write.

Origin on writes. Browsers set it on every cross-origin request and on same-origin POSTs, and page JavaScript cannot forge it. An absent Origin is a rejection rather than a pass, so a client that simply omits the header does not thereby skip the check.

A JSON-only content type on writes. The three form-encodable content types (application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, text/plain) are precisely the ones a cross-origin request may use without a preflight, which is what makes a plain cross-origin <form> POST possible with no JavaScript at all. Refusing them forces any cross-origin caller into a preflight, which this application never answers with CORS headers, so the real request is never sent.

Sec-Fetch-Site on writes. Tolerates absence, so a non-browser client used during development is not broken, and rejects any present-but-wrong value. It adds nothing against a local process, which can set the header freely; it is here because it is one line and closes a browser-side gap cheaply.

A CSRF token on writes. A server-held SynchronizerToken, embedded in the served page. See that class for why a double-submit cookie is unsound on a loopback port.

One canonical origin

The authority is a single exact spelling. If the application is reached at 127.0.0.1:8790 then localhost:8790 is not accepted, and vice versa. Accepting both doubles the surface for no benefit, and an application that links only to the spelling it accepts never notices the difference.

What this does not defend against

These are accepted residual risks, not oversights. Stating them plainly matters, because a boundary described as stopping more than it does invites the wrong decisions to be built on top of it.

  • A local process running as the same user is not defended against, and cannot be. It already holds every credential this application holds — the same keychain entries, the same config files, the same environment. It does not need this application to do anything. Nor does any of the machinery here obstruct it: everything the browser must be able to present in order for the UI to work is equally obtainable by a local HTTP client that fetches the same page first and reads the token out of it. A shared secret cannot separate "our page" from "a local program impersonating our page", because both are given the secret by the same server. This boundary raises the bar for pages in a browser; against a same-user local process it is not a control at all.
  • A malicious or compromised browser extension is not defended against. An extension can read the page, read the token out of it, and issue requests as the page. Every check here is satisfied from inside the page.
  • The human is not authenticated. There is no login. The operating-system session is the authentication; whoever is at the keyboard is the user.
  • Intent is not established. See the first section: that is a separate gate's job.
Non-browser callers

There is deliberately no path-exemption or trusted-caller list. A non-browser client that must write — including a process calling back into its own loopback port — presents the same Host, Origin, content type and token as the page does. An exemption list is the shape of API that gets one more entry added under deadline pressure until it covers the endpoint that mattered, so the boundary does not offer one.

Example:

LoopbackBoundary boundary = LoopbackBoundary.create() .authority("127.0.0.1:8790") .token(SynchronizerToken.generate()) .build(); BoundaryResult result = boundary.check(request); if (! result.isAllowed()) response.sendError(result.status(), result.message());

    • acceptsHandshakeHost

      public boolean acceptsHandshakeHost(HandshakeHosts hosts, String scheme)
      Whether a WebSocket handshake's Host values match this boundary's authority.

      A real Host header is compared as written, ignoring case, first value only: the same rule as check(HttpServletRequest). A value synthesised from an HTTP/2 (RFC 8441) handshake's request URI is compared by parsed host and port instead, filling a missing port from the handshake's scheme and the authority's from http, which is this boundary's own scheme. An authority that does not parse never matches.

      Parameters:
      hosts - The handshake's Host values. Must not be null.
      scheme - The scheme of the handshake's request URI. Can be null, which matches only a value that carries its own port.
      Returns:
      true if the handshake is addressed to this boundary's authority.

    • isStateChanging

      public static boolean isStateChanging(String method)
      Whether a request method is treated as state-changing, and therefore subject to the write checks.

      GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE are read-only. Everything else, including an unrecognized method, is state-changing.

      Delegates to MethodSafety.isSafe(String) rather than carrying its own copy of the safe-method set. The startup check that refuses a @Mutating operation bound to a safe method reads the same definition, and a boundary that disagreed with that check about which methods are writes would silently defeat both.

      Parameters:
      method - The request method. Can be null, which is treated as state-changing.
      Returns:
      true if the method is subject to the write checks.

    • selfCallHeaders

      public Map<String,String> selfCallHeaders()
      The headers an in-process client must add when calling this application's own loopback port.

      An application that calls back into itself over HTTP — a mock of an external service mounted on its own port, a background task that drives its own API — is a state-changing caller like any other, and the boundary offers it no exemption (see the class javadoc's non-browser-callers section). Rather than leaving each such caller to rediscover what the boundary wants, this returns it: the accepted Origin and the CSRF token under its configured header name.

      Host is deliberately absent. An HTTP client derives it from the request URI, so a caller already sending to this application's authority sends the right one; and Host is a restricted header that HttpClient refuses to set anyway. The caller's remaining obligation is to send Content-Type: application/json on writes, which such a client is normally doing already.

      This is not a back door. It hands the token only to code already running inside this process, which could equally read it off token(); it exists so that "call your own port correctly" does not become the argument for adding a path exemption.

      Returns:
      An immutable map of header name to value.
